after: ## How does a farm work as a system?
alt: Three farm types set out as inputs, processes and outputs: a subsistence rice plot in Sindh, a cotton farm near Vehari and a buffalo dairy near Lahore. A feedback arrow runs from outputs back to inputs.
caption: Every farm type turns inputs into outputs, and each season’s results feed back into the next.

after: ## How do kharif and rabi seasons shape production?
alt: A twelve-month calendar. Kharif crops such as cotton and rice are sown in spring or early summer and harvested in autumn; rabi crops such as wheat are sown October to December and harvested March to May. November is highlighted where cotton picking and wheat sowing overlap.
caption: Two cropping seasons share the year, and they collide in November.

after: ## How do natural and human factors affect the three named subsistence systems?
alt: Cross-section showing groundwater in the hills feeding a gently sloping underground tunnel that carries water by gravity to an oasis with date palms and vegetables. A dashed line shows how pumping by a tubewell lowers the water table below the tunnel.
caption: A karez moves groundwater by gravity with little evaporation, but falling water tables leave many dry.

after: ## How do natural and human factors affect the three named subsistence systems?
alt: A mountain profile shows transhumance: flocks move up to high summer pastures and back down to valleys or the plains in winter. Two cards below compare stall-fed buffalo and cattle on small farms with Cholistan herders moving between tobas and canal areas.
caption: Livestock is either stall-fed in one place or moved with the seasons and the water.

after: ## Which irrigation methods are used, and what are their trade-offs?
alt: Five linked stages: dams such as Tarbela and Mangla store water; barrages such as Sukkur raise the river and divert it into canals; link canals move water from western to eastern rivers; distribution canals and watercourses carry it on; field channels and bunds hold it on each plot.
caption: Water passes through five stages of engineering before it reaches a field.

after: ## What causes waterlogging and salinity, and what can be done?
alt: Cross-section of a field beside an unlined canal. Seepage and over-irrigation raise the water table; capillary action draws water up and evaporation leaves a salt crust. Below, restoration methods (SCARP tubewells, drains, flushing and gypsum) sit beside prevention methods (lining, laser levelling, measured allocation, sprinkler or drip).
caption: Too much water raises the water table; evaporation then leaves salt on the surface.

after: ## How has government tried to raise production?
alt: Five government measures (land reforms, improved seeds, research, training and credit, subsidies) lead to a balance of outcomes: yields rose, but benefits went mainly to larger farmers, much land stayed with large owners, chemicals raised costs and polluted water, and groundwater fell.
caption: Government action raised yields, but the gains were uneven and had environmental costs.
